I'll review the module for logic bugs, panics, overflow, undefined behavior, and concurrency issues, and I'll check the subtle cases against the compiler.The workspace has no crate yet, so I’m checking the language-level failure modes that are easy to get wrong: bounds checks, overflow, and the unsafe buffer code.This module is not safe to merge. Several safe functions can hit undefined behavior, `confirm` deadlocks against `place_hold` and `sweep_expired`, and the stock counters panic or wrap once `reserved` exceeds `on_hand`.

### Undefined behavior in safe functions

`SlotTable::lookup` (L185) calls `get_unchecked` on a slot index that the comment says comes from a scanner message. `assign` rejects an out-of-range slot, but `lookup` does not. If `slot >= slots.len()`, forming that reference is undefined behavior, and the caller never wrote an `unsafe` block.

`append_batch` (L194–L196) saves a raw pointer at the element just pushed, then calls `extend_from_slice`. When `tail` does not fit in the spare capacity, the `Vec` allocates a new buffer and frees the old one. The read through `first` is a use-after-free. The first SKU is already in `head`, so a normal batch of more than a handful of ids is enough to reallocate and trigger it. A batch that happens to fit only avoids the free by chance.

`decode` (L218) turns network bytes into a `&str` with `from_utf8_unchecked`. A `str` that is not UTF-8 is an invalid value, so a hostile or corrupt name is undefined behavior. The length check above it only proves the slice is long enough. The `try_into().unwrap()` calls on the `sku` and `qty` fields are safe once that length check has passed.

### Deadlock

`Service` uses three mutexes and takes them in two orders. `place_hold` (L245) and `sweep_expired` (L272) lock `warehouse` and then `holds`. `confirm` (L259) locks `holds` and then `warehouse` (L262 on the expired path, L265 on the ship path). `std::sync::Mutex` is not reentrant across threads.

One worker in `confirm`, holding `holds` and waiting for `warehouse`, and another in `sweep_expired` or `place_hold`, holding `warehouse` and waiting for `holds`, block each other permanently. `place_hold` has already run `reserve` at that point, so those units sit in `reserved` with no hold record inserted.

### Stock counters

`available` (L47) is `on_hand - reserved`. In debug builds that subtraction panics when `reserved > on_hand`. In release builds it wraps, so a later `reserve` sees a huge `have` and can overflow `reserved` with `+=` (L95). `reserve`, `low_stock`, and `place_hold` all call `available`, and a panic while `place_hold` holds the warehouse mutex poisons it. Later `lock().unwrap()` calls then panic as well.

`receive` (L81) does not add stock. The comment says an existing SKU gains `qty` on hand. `HashMap::insert` replaces the record, so the previous `on_hand`, `reserved`, name, and price are dropped. A SKU with 10 on hand and 4 reserved, received again as 3, becomes 3 on hand and 0 reserved.

`release` (L101) uses `saturating_sub` and returns `Ok` when `qty` is larger than `reserved`. It clears every reservation on that SKU, including units held for other callers. Those units can be reserved again while the old holds still exist. `ship` and `reserve` both report `Insufficient` for the same kind of mismatch.

`record_loss` (L120) subtracts `lost` from `on_hand` with no check. `lost > on_hand` panics in debug and wraps in release. A smaller loss still breaks the invariant: on hand 10, reserved 8, loss 5 leaves on hand 5 and reserved 8, and `record_loss` returns `Ok`. `available` then panics or wraps.

`ship` (L112) only checks `qty` against `reserved`. After the state above, `ship(6)` passes that check, decrements `reserved`, then evaluates `on_hand -= 6`. Debug builds panic before the assignment, so `reserved` is already reduced and `on_hand` is not. Release builds wrap `on_hand` to a value near `u32::MAX`.

`total_value` (L127) does `on_hand as u64 * price_cents` and sums the products with `+`. Either the multiply or the sum panics in debug and wraps in release once the catalog is large. One SKU with `on_hand == u32::MAX` and `price_cents` above about 4.29e9 is enough to overflow the product. A wrapped `on_hand` from `record_loss` or `ship` makes the reported value nonsense.

### Deltas

`deltas` (L156–L157) walks `0..prices.len()` and reads `prices[i + 1]`. For a non-empty slice the last step is one past the end and panics. An empty slice returns an empty `Vec` because the range is empty. The same subtraction overflows `i64` in debug (wraps in release) for inputs such as `[i64::MAX, -1]`, before the out-of-bounds read is reached. The allocation size on L155 is `len - 1`, which matches the intended number of gaps.

`moving_average` is consistent with its assert: a zero `window` panics, and a positive window produces one average per full span.

### Wire format

`encode` (L204) stores `name.len() as u8`, which keeps only the low 8 bits, then writes every name byte (L205). A 256-byte name is tagged with length 0. `decode` then reads an empty name and takes `sku` and `qty` from the first 8 bytes of the name. Names of 255 bytes or less round-trip.

### Holds

`place_hold` reserves first, then builds `Instant::now() + ttl` (L253). `Instant + Duration` panics when the sum does not fit in the platform clock. `Duration::MAX`, and any timeout past the remaining range of `Instant` (on the order of a few centuries), panics after `reserve` has succeeded and before `holds.insert`. Both the warehouse and holds mutexes are held, so they poison, and nothing is left in the map for `sweep_expired` to return those units.

`confirm` (L260) removes the hold before `release` or `ship` finishes. On the success path that is easy to miss, because a consistent service still has `reserved >= hold.qty`. If `ship` returns `Insufficient`, the id is already gone, `sweep_expired` will not see it, and the units stay in `reserved`. The same removal-before-update applies when `ship` panics on the `on_hand` subtraction.

The three unit tests cover a small reserve-and-ship, a short ASCII name, and one parse. They do not reach these paths.

ISSUES:
L47: unchecked `on_hand - reserved` panics in debug or wraps in release when reserved exceeds stock
L81: `receive` replaces an existing SKU, discarding previous `on_hand` and `reserved`
L101: `release` saturates and returns `Ok` when `qty` exceeds `reserved`, clearing other reservations
L112: `ship` subtracts `qty` from `on_hand` with no `on_hand` check, panicking or wrapping, and already updated `reserved` if it panics
L120: `record_loss` subtracts `lost` from `on_hand` unchecked and can leave `reserved > on_hand`
L127: `total_value` multiplies and sums `u64` values that overflow (debug panic, release wrap)
L156: `deltas` iterates `0..len` and panics on `prices[i + 1]` for every non-empty slice
L157: `i64` price subtraction overflows (debug panic, release wrap)
L185: `lookup` uses `get_unchecked` on an untrusted slot; an out-of-range index is undefined behavior
L196: `append_batch` reads a pointer into `buf` after `extend_from_slice` may have freed that buffer (use-after-free)
L204: name length is truncated to `u8` while the full name is written, so names longer than 255 bytes decode as a different record
L218: `from_utf8_unchecked` on network bytes is undefined behavior when the name is not UTF-8
L253: `Instant::now() + ttl` panics on overflow after `reserve`, leaking the reservation and poisoning both mutexes
L259: `confirm` locks `holds` then `warehouse`; `place_hold` (L245) and `sweep_expired` (L272) lock `warehouse` then `holds`, so they deadlock
L260: the hold is removed before `ship` or `release` finishes, so a failed ship leaves units reserved with no hold id

Reviewing the Rust inventory service for real defects: logic errors, panics, integer overflow, undefined behavior, memory safety issues, and concurrency problems.

`Item::available` subtracts `reserved` from `on_hand`. This can panic in debug mode or wrap in release mode if reserved exceeds on hand.

`record_loss` can reduce `on_hand` below `reserved` without bounds checking. `release` uses saturating_sub, so it silently ignores excess releases.

`receive` replaces the entire `Item` instead of adding quantity to existing stock. This wipes prior `on_hand` and `reserved` values for existing SKUs.

`release` silently clamps excess releases to zero via `saturating_sub`. It returns success even when no reservation exists, which can make available stock appear higher than it actually is.

`ship` and `reserve` both enforce bounds, but `release` does not. This inconsistency means callers cannot rely on `release` to detect double-releases or missing reservations.

`ship` subtracts `qty` from `on_hand` without checking that the result stays non-negative. If `record_loss` previously broke the invariant where `reserved` never exceeds `on_hand`, this can panic in debug or wrap to a huge value in release.

`record_loss` can reduce `on_hand` below zero without checking bounds, causing a panic in debug or wrap-around in release. It also ignores reserved stock, so losing reserved units leaves holds believing those items still exist.

`total_value` multiplies `on_hand` by `price_cents` and sums the products. Both operations can overflow a `u64`, causing a panic in debug or wrap-around in release for large inventories.

`low_stock` calls `available()` without checking bounds, so it will panic if `reserved` ever exceeds `on_hand`.

`moving_average` panics via an `assert!` when the window is zero. This is a hard failure on invalid input rather than returning an error or empty result.

The `moving_average` loop is correct when the window is positive. If the window exceeds the daily count, it returns an empty vector. The sum of daily counts into a `u64` is safe because slice lengths are memory-limited.

`moving_average` can overflow its `u64` sum when the window reaches `2^32` and every daily count is `u32::MAX`. The product exceeds `u64::MAX`, so the total wraps instead of panicking.

`deltas` panics when given an empty slice because the loop reads `prices[i + 1]` at index 0, which is out of bounds.

`deltas` also panics on any non-empty slice because the loop reads `prices[i + 1]` at the final index. The subtraction `prices[i + 1] - prices[i]` can overflow `i64`, causing a panic in debug or wrap-around in release.

`SlotTable::lookup` uses `get_unchecked` on the slot index without bounds checking. Since the slot comes from untrusted scanner input, this is undefined behavior and a memory safety defect.

`append_batch` takes a raw pointer to the first element after pushing it, then calls `extend_from_slice`. If the vector reallocates, that pointer becomes dangling and dereferencing it is undefined behavior.

`append_batch` unnecessarily uses a raw pointer to the just-pushed element. The `head` value was already copied, so returning it directly would eliminate the unsafe code entirely.

`encode` truncates item names to 255 bytes by casting the length to `u8`. Names longer than 255 bytes wrap around in the length field while the full name is still written, corrupting the wire format.

`encode` silently corrupts names longer than 255 bytes. The length byte wraps to zero while the full name is written, so `decode` misreads the remaining payload as SKU and quantity. This is a real data corruption defect.

`decode` uses `from_utf8_unchecked` on the name bytes. Untrusted network input can contain invalid UTF-8, so this is undefined behavior. It should use `from_utf8` and return a Malformed error instead.

`Service::place_hold` acquires three separate mutexes in sequence: warehouse, holds, then next_id. This creates a lock ordering dependency that could deadlock if callers acquire the same locks in a different order.

`Service::confirm` acquires the `holds` mutex before the `warehouse` mutex. This reverses the lock order used by `place_hold`, which holds `warehouse` first and then `holds`. The mismatch creates a deadlock risk if callers acquire the same locks in opposite order.

`sweep_expired` acquires the `warehouse` mutex before the `holds` mutex. This completes the ABBA deadlock cycle with `place_hold` and `confirm`.

`confirm` removes the hold from the map before checking expiry or shipping. If `ship` fails, the hold is already gone and cannot be retried.

If `ship` fails after the hold is removed, the reservation stays locked forever because the hold no longer exists. The SKU was never released back to available stock.

`receive()` replaces the entire `Item`, which resets `reserved` to zero while any existing holds still reference that SKU. If a hold was placed before receiving, `confirm()` later tries to ship and fails with `Insufficient` because the reservation no longer exists, yet the hold record is already gone.

`next_id` increments without bounds checking. After `u64::MAX` holds, the counter wraps to zero and may collide with existing live hold IDs.

`place_hold` adds `ttl` to `Instant::now()`. If the duration is very large, this can panic because `Instant + Duration` overflows.

`Instant + Duration` panics when the resulting time cannot be represented, so a very large TTL is a real panic bug. The `.unwrap()` on `Mutex::lock()` can also panic if another thread poisoned the lock, though this is idiomatic Rust.

A panic while holding the warehouse lock poisons it, causing every subsequent service call to fail. The root defects are the panics and deadlocks; the poisoned unwrap is a secondary cascade risk.

`place_hold` holds the warehouse lock while incrementing `next_id`, which widens the deadlock window. If `reserve` succeeds but a panic occurs before `holds.insert`, the stock stays reserved with no hold record.

`sweep_expired` ignores `release` errors when dropping expired holds. If release fails, the hold is removed but the stock stays reserved.

`release` uses saturating subtraction, so releasing more stock than is reserved succeeds without error. This silently desynchronizes the hold map from actual inventory.

`record_loss` does not verify that the lost quantity is within `on_hand`, and it never adjusts reserved stock. This can silently desynchronize inventory from actual holdings.

`Item` fields are public, so callers can set `reserved` above `on_hand` directly. This breaks the inventory invariant and causes `available()` to panic.

`confirm` holds the `holds` mutex while calling warehouse methods, so a slow `ship` call blocks all other hold operations. This is a performance bottleneck rather than a logic defect.

`total_value` sums `u64` quantities with `sum()`, which panics in debug mode if the total overflows `u64::MAX`.

`low_stock` calls `available()` on every SKU, so if any item has `reserved` greater than `on_hand`, the function panics.

`SlotTable::lookup` dereferences `Option<Sku>` via `get_unchecked` without bounds checking. This is undefined behavior when the slot index is out of range, though it is safe if the index is valid.

`place_hold` drops the `next_id` lock before inserting into the holds map, yet still holds the `holds` lock. If a later thread tries to acquire `warehouse` while holding `holds`, it deadlocks because `place_hold` already owns `warehouse`.

`confirm`'s expired path calls `release` with `?`, but the hold is already removed from the map. If `release` saturates because `reserved` is too low, the function returns `Expired` without error and the reservation stays locked. The ship path is the one that actually errors and leaks the reservation.

`reserve` adds `qty` to `reserved` without checking for overflow. The `available()` guard normally prevents this, but in release mode it wraps around when `reserved` exceeds `on_hand`, allowing the addition to silently overflow.

`record_loss` wraps `on_hand` to a huge value in release mode. This inflates `total_value` and allows callers to reserve far more stock than exists.

`append_batch` dereferences a dangling pointer when re-reading the batch head value, which is undefined behavior.

`encode` writes the full name bytes but stores only a truncated length, so the wire format contains a name longer than its declared size. This is a real encoding bug.

The dangling pointer in `append_batch` is conditional: it only triggers if the vector reallocates during `extend_from_slice`. Even then, the compiler may miscompile other paths because undefined behavior invalidates all assumptions.

The dangling pointer in `append_batch` is not limited to reallocation. Rust's Tree Borrows model can invalidate the raw pointer from `as_ptr()` when a mutable borrow occurs during `extend_from_slice`, even without a buffer move. This makes the undefined behavior unconditional.

The dangling pointer in `append_batch` is a definite defect because the code never reserves capacity before taking the raw pointer, so reallocation is guaranteed to occur. The standard fix is to reserve space first or simply use the head value directly.

Service does not expose `release` or `record_loss`, so external callers cannot directly manipulate the inner warehouse. After construction, only Service methods mutate inventory, and holds are tracked entirely within the service. This narrows the leak path: a failed ship can only occur when `reserved` is smaller than the hold quantity, which happens when holds are released or expired before shipping.

The `ship` panic is likely unreachable through the public API. Service never exposes `record_loss`, `release`, or `receive`, so external callers cannot reduce `on_hand` below a hold's reserved quantity.

`deltas` panics when given a single element, because the loop expects at least two values.

`deltas` panics on the final loop iteration for any non-empty input, so it never returns successfully.

`deltas` panics on the final loop iteration for any non-empty input, so it never returns a result. `moving_average` is off-by-one safe; its assert is a panic, not a logic defect.

`receive` replaces the entire item instead of adding to `on_hand`, silently discarding `reserved`, name, and price. This contradicts its documentation.

`from_utf8_unchecked` on network bytes is undefined behavior if the name is not valid UTF-8.

`Instant::now() + ttl` panics when the TTL duration overflows `Instant`. This occurs after `reserve` has already succeeded, so reserved units leak and the mutexes are poisoned.

`confirm` removes the hold record from the map before calling `ship` or `release`. If that call fails, the reservation is leaked and the hold cannot be retried.

`next_id` can wrap to an existing hold ID. The new hold overwrites the old record in the map, leaking its reservation and dropping the prior hold.

`receive` overwrites an existing item instead of adding to `on_hand`, so any reserved holds for that SKU become orphaned. If the caller later mutates the warehouse directly, those units are released back into inventory while still logically reserved.

`release` silently succeeds when the caller tries to return more units than were reserved. The tests do not catch this because they only exercise the normal case.

The `append_batch` dangling pointer is conditional on reallocation. If the buffer has enough capacity, the read is valid and the undefined behavior is avoided. Still, the code never reserves space first, so reallocation is guaranteed and the bug is definite.

The `moving_average` assert is an explicit precondition, not a defect. The `next_id` wrap-around is impractical and the mutex poison is idiomatic. Public fields, `decode` unwrap, missing price or reserved in `encode`, and `low_stock` are not real defects.

`record_loss` panics when `lost` exceeds `on_hand`. It also silently corrupts the inventory invariant when `lost` is between `on_hand` and `on_hand + reserved`, because the code subtracts from `on_hand` without checking that `reserved` stays non-negative. This later causes `available()` and `ship` to panic.

`SlotTable::lookup` returns `None` for both empty slots and out-of-bounds indices, so callers cannot distinguish a missing slot from an invalid index. The function should return `Result` instead of `Option` to expose the error.

`available()` can wrap to a huge value in release mode, so items with `reserved` exceeding `on_hand` may never appear as low stock. The `receive` log is also pushed even when it destroys existing reservations.

`place_hold` holds the warehouse lock for the entire duration of the call, so `next_id` is never accessed concurrently. Duplicate hold IDs are therefore impossible.

A deadlock between `confirm` and `place_hold` or `sweep_expired` is possible. `confirm` locks the holds map before the warehouse lock, while `place_hold` locks the warehouse before the holds map. If both threads acquire their first lock, neither can proceed.

While deadlocked, any stock already reserved by `place_hold` remains locked indefinitely. Those units stay unavailable until the deadlock resolves.

The `append_batch` dangling pointer is conditional on reallocation. Rust's vector growth algorithm allocates capacity 4 for a `u32` buffer, so a batch of four elements fits exactly and never triggers the bug. A batch of five elements forces reallocation, which causes the undefined behavior. Miri would catch this when the buffer grows.

The `append_batch` raw pointer is unsafe even when the vector does not reallocate. Rust's `Vec::as_ptr` documentation implies the pointer remains valid for the vector's length, but recent Stacked Borrows models and Miri treat this pattern as undefined behavior regardless of whether the buffer moves.

`reserve` checks `available()` before adding to `reserved`, so a wrapped `available` value cannot overflow `reserved` during normal execution. The integer overflow at line 95 is therefore unreachable through the public API.

The wrapped `available` value lets `reserve` add past `u32::MAX`, so `reserved += qty` at line 95 can overflow in release mode. This will be listed as a distinct issue.

The zero-window assert in `moving_average` is an explicit precondition, not a defect. The `next_id` wrap-around is theoretical and will be omitted. The hold removal at line 260 will be included since a failed ship leaves the reservation state corrupted.

If `ship` panics on an underflow, the reserved quantity is already reduced and the hold record is removed from the map. The stock becomes available again, so the units are not leaked; only the log is lost and the mutex is poisoned.

The `ship` underflow panic poisons both the warehouse and holds mutexes, so `Service` deadlocks. The `remove-before-ship` bug is a logic defect: if `qty` exceeds `item.reserved`, the reservation is leaked because the hold record was already removed from the map.

`place_hold` reserves stock before acquiring the holds lock, so a later failure leaves the reservation committed without a hold record to release it. The `Instant` overflow panic is the concrete failure that triggers this leak.

If the holds mutex is already poisoned, `place_hold` can still panic after reserving stock. The reservation is committed but the hold record is never inserted, so another reservation leaks. This creates a cascade where a single poison event can corrupt multiple reservations.

The `deltas` vector reserves capacity for `prices.len() - 1`, but the loop pushes `prices.len()` elements. The index out-of-bounds panic occurs before any reallocation, so the buffer never grows and the capacity mismatch is harmless.

The `deltas` capacity mismatch is an off-by-one error, not a separate defect. The `moving_average` loop panics on the first iteration when the difference overflows, before the index out-of-bounds error can occur.

`sweep_expired` samples `Instant::now()` before acquiring the warehouse and holds locks. A hold that expires while a thread waits for those locks is still swept, because the captured timestamp is already in the past.

`encode` truncates `name.len()` to `u8` with a plain cast, so names longer than 255 bytes silently wrap around. Using `try_into` would catch this.

The `encode` length field is a byte count, but the encoder still writes the full name slice. When the name exceeds 255 bytes, the decoder reads an empty string and misinterprets the next eight bytes as SKU and quantity. This silent corruption is a protocol-level bug.

`get_unchecked` is undefined behavior when the index is out of bounds. `release` silently succeeds on over-release, unlike `ship` which errors.

`release` should error when the quantity exceeds the reserved amount, but it currently succeeds. This allows over-release to zero out other orders' reservations and breaks audit accuracy. `record_loss` also subtracts stock unconditionally without logging the failure.

`record_loss` can break the `on_hand >= reserved` invariant without panicking. If the lost quantity exceeds available stock, `available()` later underflows and panics.

`total_value` uses `Iterator::sum` on `u64`, which panics in debug mode when the running total overflows. The unchecked subtraction in `record_loss` is a logic defect even when the lost quantity does not exceed available stock, because it still breaks the `on_hand >= reserved` invariant.

The `sweep_expired` closure ignores the `Result` from `wh.release`, so a failed release silently drops stock. This is a logic defect. The `Item` snapshot clone is safe because the caller owns it and cannot mutate the warehouse state.

`Service::new` accepts any `Warehouse`, so an existing instance with inconsistent state could be passed in. `ship` would then fail because `place_hold` already checked `available()` before adding to `reserved`.

I am compiling small tests to verify subtle bugs before finalizing the review. I have confirmed that `sort_by_key` is not a defect. I am checking whether `append_batch` always triggers reallocation and if `from_utf8_unchecked` causes undefined behavior.

I confirmed that `Instant` addition panics on overflow and that integer overflow behaves differently in release versus debug builds. I also identified a use-after-free bug in `append_batch`: the unsafe pointer arithmetic assumes the vector will not reallocate, but `extend_from_slice` can trigger reallocation and invalidate the raw pointer.

I am checking whether `append_batch` violates Rust's Stacked Borrows rules even without reallocation. The `Vec::as_ptr` documentation warns that mutating the container can invalidate pointers, and `as_mut_ptr` is required for writes.

The unsafe pointer in `append_batch` may be invalid under Tree Borrows. A mutable borrow of the vector from `extend_from_slice` can invalidate raw pointers derived from shared references, even without reallocation.

Miri flags this exact pattern as undefined behavior. The temporary borrow ends before `extend_from_slice` mutably borrows the vector, so the raw pointer is invalidated by the reborrow even without reallocation.

The documented contract for `Vec::as_ptr` is that the pointer remains valid only until reallocation. The `append_batch` function violates this by pushing elements without first reserving capacity, so the raw pointer becomes invalid as soon as the vector grows.

I am now calculating the exact capacity thresholds that trigger reallocation in `append_batch`. If the vector already has enough spare capacity, neither `push` nor `extend_from_slice` will reallocate. The pointer remains valid. I am checking the Rust allocator's growth algorithm to confirm when reallocation actually occurs.

The Rust allocator's `min_non_zero_cap` function sets the initial capacity for a `u32` vector to 4. An empty buffer can therefore hold two elements without reallocation, but a batch of five elements forces reallocation and triggers the use-after-free in `append_batch`. This confirms the bug is a genuine undefined behavior when the batch exceeds the growth step.

I confirmed the exact failure path in `append_batch`: after `push` doubles capacity, `extend_from_slice` can reallocate again and leave the raw pointer dangling. The returned SKU may still read the old value by accident, but this is undefined behavior. I am now checking the documentation for `from_utf8_unchecked`.

`from_utf8_unchecked` is a memory-safety defect. It assumes valid UTF-8 without checking, so untrusted input triggers undefined behavior. Invalid UTF-8 should return `Malformed` instead of invoking UB.

`get_unchecked` is also a definite undefined behavior bug when the slot index exceeds the vector length.

`encode` truncates lengths to `u8`. A 256-byte name becomes length 0. The full string is still written. `decode` reads the wrong length and corrupts parsing. This is a logic error.
